claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles under the stated service regimes is governed by the degree of local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering can be controlled through in situ characterization techniques.
Local chemical ordering can be controlled through tailored synthesis conditions.
X-ray powder diffraction and X-ray absorption spectroscopy can monitor nanoparticle formation and properties during synthesis.
The degree of local chemical ordering influences nanoparticle crystal structure.
The degree of local chemical ordering influences nanoparticle lattice strain.
The degree of local chemical ordering influences nanoparticle defect density.
Changes in crystal structure, lattice strain, and defect density caused by local chemical ordering affect structural and chemical stability.
Nanoparticles with higher degrees of local chemical ordering will exhibit improved structural and chemical stability during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
Nanoparticles with higher degrees of local chemical ordering will exhibit improved structural and chemical stability during thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles synthesized without in situ characterization and tailored synthesis conditions constitute the baseline.
The proposed hypothesis is limited to catalytic operation at 773–1173 K, thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, and multi-element near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticle compositions.
Failure of more highly ordered nanoparticles to show improved stability relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes in situ characterization as a means of controlling local chemical ordering, whereas the intervention describes the same techniques only as passive monitoring tools. No feedback or synthesis adjustment is specified that would make characterization itself a controlled intervention on ordering.

The intervention specifies in situ characterization, but the baseline differs in both characterization and unspecified tailored synthesis conditions. This bundles multiple changes and prevents attribution of an outcome specifically to local chemical ordering.
